headline: Three theories for sake — “flourish”, “ward off” cold illness, or a corruption of kushi — and none is settled.
A pot named for a snack: 鍋 is na (“small snack”) + he (“pot”), with rendaku turning he into be.
Shio is cognate with Ainu sippo, and the Nippo Jisho of 1603 shows it already softened.
Vovin considers miso a borrowing from Koreanic — compare meju — and a 938 source calls it a “Korean sauce”.
An egg is a “ball child”: 玉 (tama) + 子 (ko), with ko voiced to go.
Japanese for “pencil” is a calque of English “lead pencil”, built from a Chinese word.
Fuyu began with a p: Old Japanese puyu, from Proto-Japonic *puyu.
Samui was samushi, and from the Muromachi period it was sometimes pronounced sabushi.
Snow is yuki, but one eastern-dialect song in the Man'yōshū has yoki, and some reconstruct *yoki as the ancestor.
Ice is a verb turned noun: kōri is the stem of 凍る (kōru, “to freeze”).
Smoke was keburi before it was kemuri, and the shorter kemu is a clipping attested since 1275.
Fire has a hidden twin: hi is an apophonic form of ho, as ki (“tree”) pairs with ko-.
Flame is “fire's ear of grain”: 火 (ho) + の (no) + 穂 (ho).
Yu goes back to Proto-Japonic *yu and appears in both the Kojiki (712 CE) and the Man'yōshū.
Japanese ストーブ is borrowed straight from English stove.
Japanese セーター is borrowed straight from English sweater.
Who borrowed from whom? Some Japanese sources say kutsu comes from Korean gudu; some Korean sources say the reverse.
A cough is a verb stem, and seki is cognate with 堰 (seki, “dam”).
House took four steps from ipe to ie, and Old Korean may have a cousin.
A wall is a “place divider”: 処 (ka, “place”) + 重 (he, “division”), with he voiced to be.
Yuka meant “bed” in the Nihon Shoki, and a 1668 scholar derived it from “not going”.
Mise is short for misedana: miseru (“to show”) + tana (“shelf”).
A mirror is “shadow-seeing”: kaga (影, “shadow; image”) + mi (見, “seeing”).
Hoshi began as posi, from Proto-Japonic *pəsi.
Tsuki was once tuki, and Wiktionary notes a vowel alternation between its standalone and combining forms.
One dictionary says neko is a shortening of nekoma, but neko is attested in 794 and nekoma only in 918.
Derivation uncertain: from “to leave”, from “house” + “sleep”, from 狗 — or borrowed from some unknown language.
Cow is Proto-Japonic *‹u,o›si: the reconstruction cannot decide between u and o.
Was it muma? Wiktionary notes the “ma” horse words across Asia, even English mare, but says no consensus exists.
A bird (tori) may be kin to the Korean word for chicken, 닭 (dak).
